question_text: According to the course material, Module 2 is titled:
option_a: History and Development of Philosophy
explanation: Module 2 History and Development of Philosophy covers ancient, medieval and renaissance, modern, contemporary movements, and the idea of African philosophy.

question_text: According to the course material, the revolution in modern philosophical thought was sparked by the French philosopher and mathematician:
option_a: René Descartes
explanation: The revolution that took place in philosophical thought in these two ages was sparked by the French philosopher and mathematician René Descartes.

question_text: According to the course material, Descartes was the first figure in the loose movement known as:
option_a: Rationalism
explanation: He was the first figure in the loose movement known as Rationalism, and much of subsequent Western philosophy can be seen as a response to his ideas.

question_text: According to the course material, Descartes' method was known as methodological skepticism and its aim was to:
option_a: dispel skepticism and arrive at certain knowledge
option_b: prove that no knowledge is possible
explanation: His method was known as methodological skepticism and its aim was to dispel Skepticism and arrive at certain knowledge.

question_text: According to the course material, Descartes' method was to remove everything about which there could be even:
option_a: a suspicion of doubt
explanation: This method was to remove everything about which there could be even a suspicion of doubt.

question_text: According to the course material, Empiricism represents the belief that the origin of all knowledge is:
option_a: sense experience
explanation: Empiricism represents the belief that the origin of all knowledge is sense experience.

question_text: According to the course material, in England the Contemporary age began in the:
option_a: 19th Century
explanation: In England, the Contemporary age began in the 19th Century.

question_text: According to the course material, Utilitarianism grew out of the:
option_a: British Empiricist tradition of the previous century
explanation: It recorded a very different kind of philosophy, which grew out of the British Empiricist tradition of the previous century. One of such philosophy is the Utilitarianism movement.

question_text: According to the course material, Utilitarianism was founded by the social reformer Jeremy Bentham and popularized by:
option_a: John Stuart Mill
explanation: It was founded by the social reformer Jeremy Bentham and was popularized by his even more radical protégé John Stuart Mill.

question_text: According to the course material, the idea of Utilitarianism is a type of:
option_a: Consequentialism
explanation: The idea of Utilitarianism is a type of Consequentialism. It is a kind of approach to Ethics that stresses an action's outcome or the consequence of an action.

question_text: According to the course material, Utilitarianism holds that the right action is that which would cause:
option_a: the greatest happiness of the greatest number
option_b: the least happiness of the fewest people
explanation: It holds that the right action is that which would cause the greatest happiness of the greatest number.

question_text: According to the course material, Mill refined Utilitarianism to stress:
option_a: the quality not just the quantity of happiness, and intellectual and moral pleasures over more physical forms
option_b: only physical pleasure counted by quantity
explanation: This theory was refined by Mill to stress the quality not just the quantity of happiness, and intellectual and moral pleasures over more physical forms.

question_text: According to the course material, Mill counselled that coercion in society is only justifiable:
option_a: either to defend ourselves or to defend others from harm (the harm principle)
explanation: He counselled that coercion in society is only justifiable either to defend ourselves or to defend others from harm (the harm principle).

question_text: According to the course material, Unit 4 on contemporary movements discusses Pragmatism, Logical Positivism, and the two traditions:
option_a: Analytic and Continental philosophy
explanation: We shall be talking about Pragmatism, Logical Positivism and the two philosophical movements trending in the contemporary age, which are Analytic and Continental philosophy.

question_text: According to the course material, under Continental philosophy the unit lists:
option_a: Phenomenology and Existentialism
explanation: The contents list 3.5 Continental Philosophy, 3.5.1 Phenomenology, 3.5.2 Existentialism.

question_text: According to the course material, the search for African philosophy is dominated by the need for:
option_a: a new identity authentic to Africans and distinct from those imposed by western culture and tradition
option_b: a copy of only Hegel's lectures
option_c: the abolition of all African thought
explanation: The search for African philosophy is dominated by the need for a new identity authentic to Africans and distinct from those imposed by western culture and tradition.

question_text: According to the course material, some Western scholars like Hegel believed that Africans:
option_a: are people against which all reason could be contrasted
option_b: were the only humans who could reason
explanation: Some Western scholars like Hegel believed that Africans are people against which all reason could be contrasted.

question_text: According to the course material, the Western opinion that Africans cannot philosophize is examined in order to:
option_a: show the meaning of African philosophy
option_b: prove Hegel was the last word
explanation: This Unit is therefore an examination of these Western opinion on African philosophy with a view to show the meaning of African philosophy.

question_text: According to the course material, the contention whether there is African philosophy has been laid to rest given:
option_a: various African philosophers' views expounded in the unit
option_c: the absence of any African writer
explanation: The contention of whether there is African philosophy or not has been laid to rest given the various African philosophers' views that have been expounded in this unit.

question_text: According to the course material, given the growth of African philosophy in contemporary time, the philosophy is assuming:
option_a: the same status with western philosophy
explanation: Given the level of the growth of African philosophy and its waves in the contemporary time the philosophy is assuming the same status with the western philosophy.

question_text: According to the course material, a reference listed for African philosophy is Hountondji's:
option_a: African Philosophy: Myth and Reality
explanation: Houtundji, P. African Philosophy: Myth and Reality, Bloomington & Indianapolis, Indiana University Press, 1996.

question_text: According to the course material, another listed African-philosophy text is Okere's:
option_a: African Philosophy: A Historico-Hermeneutical Investigation of the Conditions of its Possibility
explanation: Okere, Theophilus. African Philosophy: A Historico-Hermeneutical Investigation of the Conditions of its Possibility. Lanham, MD: University Press of America, 1983.

question_text: According to the course material, the general discussion of philosophy in the modern age focused on:
option_a: human survival as well as the composition of man
explanation: The general discussion of philosophy in this age was the focus on human survival as well as the composition of man. It also examined the nature of the human society as well as the history of human kind.

question_text: According to the course material, most of the 19th and 20th century movements discussed were from, but not restricted to:
option_a: America and England
explanation: It was pointed out that most of these movements were from but not so restricted to America and England, where philosophical traditions like Analytic and continental philosophy, Pragmatism, Logical positivism and many more are thriving.
